notes.text: Linezolid
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.

Resistant gram-positive infections are an important use of linezolid.

title: Chloramphenicol Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics, Mechanism of Action, Spectrum & Therapeutic Uses

notes.text: Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum antibiotic originally derived from Streptomyces venezuelae . It is now produced synthetically and is used to treat serious infections where other antibiotics are ineffective or contraindicated.
Mechanism of Action
Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit.
Prevents peptide bond formation by inhibiting peptidyl transferase activity.
Bacteriostatic, but can be bactericidal against some organisms (e.g., Haemophilus influenzae , Neisseria meningitidis ).
Spectrum of Activity
Effective against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria.
Active against anaerobes, Rickettsia , and Chlamydia .
Not effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and some Enterobacteriaceae.
Pharmacokinetics
Well absorbed orally; also available as IV and topical formulations.
Widely distributed, including cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
Metabolized in the liver by glucuronidation.
Excreted primarily by the kidneys.
Half-life: 1.5–4 hours (may be prolonged in neonates or liver dysfunction).
Serious infections: meningitis, typhoid fever, rickettsial infections, brain abscess.
Reserved for cases where safer alternatives are ineffective or contraindicated.
Topical use in eye infections (conjunctivitis).
Bone marrow suppression (dose-related and idiosyncratic aplastic anemia).
Gray baby syndrome (in neonates due to immature liver enzymes).
Gastrointestinal disturbances.
Hypersensitivity reactions.
Contraindications & Precautions
Use with caution in neonates, pregnant women, and patients with liver dysfunction.
Monitor blood counts during prolonged therapy.

title: Aminoglycosides Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Spectrum, Therapeutic Uses and Adverse Effects

notes.text: Aminoglycosides
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
30S ribosomal subunit binding leads to errors in bacterial protein synthesis.
Oxygen-dependent uptake limits activity against anaerobic organisms.
Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are major adverse effects.
Gentamicin and amikacin are examples of aminoglycosides.
Renal function and drug exposure are important monitoring considerations.

title: Glycopeptides Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Spectrum, Therapeutic Uses and Adverse Effects

notes.text: Glycopeptides
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
D-Ala-D-Ala binding interferes with bacterial cell-wall synthesis.
Vancomycin is a glycopeptide used against susceptible gram-positive organisms.
Infusion-related reactions can occur with vancomycin and are distinct from some true allergic reactions.
Renal monitoring is important during systemic treatment.
